sentences.text: This dinosaur had thin, delicate crests that likely functioned as display organs, possibly during mating events.
Unlike later tyrannosaurs, it possessed three long fingers on its hands.
It likely resembled its close relative Dilong and may have possessed a coat of primitive feathers.
One specimen was found lying on top of another along with three other theropod dinosaurs.
The juvenile individual died at six years of age while still growing.
The taxon was first described in 2006 by Xu Xing and colleagues as a new species related to Tyrannosaurus.
Fossils were discovered in the Dzungaria area of China by a joint expedition between the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology and George Washington University.
Researchers presume the immature specimen was trampled to death by the adult individual after both died.
Juvenile Guanlong exhibited features such as a proportionally shorter snout, larger orbits, larger hands, longer lower legs, and a less expanded pubic bone compared to adults.
A 2013 study classified Guanlong in the family Proceratosauridae alongside Proceratosaurus and Kileskus.
A 2014 study redefined the family Proceratosauridae to include only Guanlong, Proceratosaurus, Kileskus, and Sinotyrannus, excluding Stokesosaurus and Juratyrant.
A 2024 study placed Dilong and proceratosaurids like Guanlong outside the clade Tyrannosauroidea based on phylogenetic analysis.
Guanlong lived about 160 million years ago during the Oxfordian stage of the Late Jurassic, approximately 92 million years before Tyrannosaurus.
